subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: The social construction of crime and deviance
Theories of crime: functionalist, Marxist and interactionist
Patterns of crime by class, gender, ethnicity and age

questions.q: In sociology, 'crime' is best defined as:
options: Any behaviour that others disapprove of
An act that breaks the law and can be punished by the state
Behaviour that goes against social norms but is legal
Any act that harms another person
questions.explain: Crime refers specifically to acts that break the formal laws of a society and are punishable by the state.

questions.q: In sociology, 'deviance' is best defined as:
options: Any act that breaks the criminal law
Behaviour that goes against the norms and values of a society
Behaviour that is always punished by the courts
Crime committed only by young people
questions.explain: Deviance is behaviour that breaks social norms, whether or not it is against the law.

questions.q: To say that crime and deviance are 'socially constructed' means that:
options: They are caused only by biological factors
Definitions of them vary between different times, places and cultures
They are exactly the same in every society
Only the police can decide what is criminal
questions.explain: Social construction means that what counts as deviant or criminal is not fixed but changes across time, place and culture.

questions.q: Drinking alcohol is legal for adults in the UK, but it is illegal in some other countries. This best shows that:
options: Alcohol is always a form of deviance
What counts as deviant or criminal varies between societies, so it is socially constructed
Formal social control does not exist
questions.explain: The same act being legal in one society and illegal in another demonstrates that deviance and crime are socially constructed.

questions.q: Which sociologist argued that crime is a normal and inevitable part of every society and can even perform positive functions?
questions.explain: Durkheim, a functionalist, argued that crime is inevitable and can be functional, for example by reinforcing shared values.

questions.q: Durkheim used the term 'anomie' to describe:
options: A state of normlessness in which social rules break down
The punishment of criminals by the courts
The labelling of offenders as deviant
The economic interests of the ruling class
questions.explain: Anomie refers to a breakdown of shared norms, which Durkheim linked to higher levels of deviance.

questions.q: Robert Merton explained crime and deviance mainly using his:
questions.explain: Merton's strain theory argues that crime results from the gap between society's goals and the legitimate means available to achieve them.

questions.q: In Merton's strain theory, an 'innovator' is a person who:
options: Rejects both society's goals and the legitimate means of achieving them
Accepts society's goals but turns to illegitimate means, such as crime, to achieve them
Accepts both the goals and the approved means
Has no interest in success of any kind
questions.explain: Innovators still want success but use illegitimate means, such as theft, because legitimate routes are blocked.

questions.q: According to Marxists, the law in a capitalist society mainly protects the interests of:
questions.explain: Marxists argue that laws are made by and for the ruling class to protect their wealth and power.

questions.q: Marxists argue that crimes of the powerful, such as corporate or white-collar crime, are:
options: Punished far more harshly than working-class crime
Less likely to be detected and prosecuted than working-class crime
The main focus of official crime statistics
questions.explain: Marxists argue enforcement is selective, so the crimes of the powerful are less likely to be caught and punished.

questions.q: A student is repeatedly labelled 'a troublemaker' by teachers. He begins to see himself this way and misbehaves more as a result. This best illustrates:
questions.explain: Interactionists argue a label can become a self-fulfilling prophecy when a person acts in line with how they have been defined.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a formal agency of social control?
questions.explain: Formal social control is carried out by official agencies such as the police, courts and prisons that enforce written laws.

questions.q: In the study of social control, a 'sanction' is best defined as:
options: A reward or punishment that encourages people to conform to norms
questions.explain: Sanctions can be positive (rewards) or negative (punishments) and are used to encourage conformity.

questions.q: A father praises his daughter for helping with the housework, encouraging her to behave that way again. He is applying a:
questions.explain: Praise from a family member is an informal positive sanction, rewarding conformity to shared norms.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes informal social control?
options: Control through written laws and official punishments
Control through unwritten rules, enforced by agencies such as the family and peer groups
Control carried out only by the police and courts
questions.explain: Informal social control relies on unwritten norms enforced by agencies such as the family, peers and the media.

questions.q: In England and Wales, official crime statistics are mainly based on:
questions.explain: Official crime statistics are largely made up of crimes reported to and recorded by the police.

questions.q: The 'dark figure of crime' refers to:
options: The amount of crime that is not reported to or recorded by the police
The most violent crimes in society
Crime that appears in official statistics
questions.explain: The dark figure is the hidden crime missing from official statistics because it is not reported or recorded.

questions.q: Which statement is consistent with the pattern between age and crime shown in official statistics?
options: Offending is spread evenly across all age groups
Recorded offending tends to peak among people in their teens and early twenties
Most recorded offenders are over the age of 60
Young children commit the majority of recorded crime
questions.explain: Statistics show recorded offending is highest among young people, peaking in the teens and early twenties before declining.

questions.q: Some sociologists argue that certain minority ethnic groups are over-represented in crime statistics mainly because of:
options: Possible discrimination and bias within the criminal justice system
A lack of interest in official statistics
questions.explain: Many sociologists argue the pattern partly reflects bias and discrimination in policing and the courts rather than differences in offending.

questions.q: A female offender receives a more lenient sentence than a male offender who committed a similar crime, and a sociologist explains this by arguing the courts treat women more favourably. This idea is known as:
questions.explain: The chivalry thesis argues the criminal justice system tends to treat women more leniently than men.

specSource: AQA GCSE Sociology (8192) specification; The Sociology of Crime & Deviance
